items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: I went to hear Lee Konitz one night. At that time he was a big jazz player and everything. And he was talking to me and he said, you know, man, just because I'm a jazz player, you know, I can read and spell. If there are any gigs you'd like to do, I'd appreciate it if you'd fix me up.

ctx.x: you to talk about this. What about the words, "studio musician"? How do you feel about that?

Well, it's kind of a put-down word. But studio musicians, it really is sort of a jack of all trades, but not necessarily master of none, because most of the studio musicians I know are the top players and many of them were the top jazz players. It was always a critical word.

Now, I know when I left Benny Goodman's band, I left it in 1943 and I went into the studios. I had a good friend, Gil Evans, who used to needle me all of the time about it. And he'd see me up the Union, collecting my checks, and he'd make corny remarks, "$1 million, $2 million," or something. And I always felt a little apologetic about it. But I had a family to support and I have children, and I didn't believe that I had the right to go out on the road and enjoy myself playing in jazz bands or whatever and leave…
